title: Trump takes aim at Russia's energy sector with sanctions bill
description: US President Donald Trump has signed a sweeping sanctions bill, taking aim at Russia's economy by punishing major purchasers of its oil and gas. The b
body: US President Donald Trump has signed a sweeping sanctions bill, taking aim at Russia's economy by punishing major purchasers of its oil and gas. The bill, passed by the US House of Representatives earlier this week, gives Trump broad powers to levy tariffs of up to 100% on the top five purchasers of Russian oil and gas – most significantly China and India.At Trump's behest, the bill also extends to Iran's energy and weapons sectors. The bill is named after the late Senator Lindsey Graham, one of Ukraine's staunchest defenders in Washington before his death on 11 July. The 48-page bill, formally titled the Lindsey O Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, includes exceptions for countries that import less than 15% of their natural gas from Russia and are working to lessen their dependency. Additionally, the bill includes sanctions against Russian President Vladimir Putin, senior figures within the Russian government as well as banks and other financial institutions and Russia's "shadow fleet" of tankers used to circumvent existing sanctions. Senator Richard Blumenthal, a New York Democrat, previously described the legislation as "scorching sanctions" which would "throttle Putin's war machine". Data from the Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, or CREA, shows that China accounted for 50% of Russian crude exports between December 2022 and August 2026, followed by India at 37%. Turkey and the European Union each accounted for 5% during the same time period, although Russian energy exports to the EU have been decreasing. Senator Graham had long sought to push the Trump administration to do more to punish Russia for the war that followed its invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. The bill also had the support of Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who praised its passage by the House of Representatives earlier this week. "It is symbolic that the US House of Representatives' passage of Lindsey Graham's sanctions bill took place on the night of yet another Russian attack on Ukraine involving ballistic missiles, other missiles, and drones," Zelensky wrote on Telegram on 17 September. Graham, 71, died on 11 July of an "aortic dissection" caused by cardiovascular disease shortly after returning from a trip to Kyiv. "He died doing the work he was born to do," Trump said at the time. Prior to his death, he was widely considered one of Ukraine's fiercest allies on Capitol Hill, at a time when Republicans were bitterly divided over the extent of US involvement abroad and the amount of aid being given to Ukraine.

schema.headline: Trump takes aim at Russia's energy sector with sanctions bill

title: Russian hybrid attacks against Europe intensifying, says Macron
description: Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, de
body: Hybrid warfare or hybrid attacks are loose terms which tend to describe non-military methods, for example cyberattacks, sabotage or misinformation, designed to exert pressure and destabilise an adversary.These are quite often employed using proxies, but Russia always denies involvement in such attacks despite growing evidence to the contrary.The French president was speaking to journalists after meeting party leaders to discuss the security impact of the wars in the Middle East and Ukraine.Macron mentioned last month's drone attack on Leipzig airport in Germany, blamed on Russia, and remarks by Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk suggesting Russia was planning drone and missile strikes against Poland and other countries on Nato's eastern flank."In recent weeks, the Russian hybrid threat against Europeans and against France has intensified," he said."The intent is to intimidate us and break our effort to support Ukraine. The result will be the exact opposite. We are not intimidated because we know that our security today and tomorrow is at stake in Ukraine."On Thursday Tusk told Polish MPs that Russian plans included strikes by drones and missiles on countries supporting Ukraine. He said there was a "real risk" of such strikes on the territory of Nato countries, with Moscow then claiming that they were "accidental", in an attempt to split the alliance.Last Sunday, a Russian drone hit a passenger train near the Ukraine-Poland border shortly after former UK Prime Minister Boris Johnson and top European security officials had passed through along the same line.Ukraine said all the passengers had been evacuated just minutes before the strike at Yahodyn, which hit the train's engine.There have also been a number of suspicious fires at defence facilities from Italy to Estonia, with some of the affected countries blaming Russia.Russian President Vladimir Putin has repeatedly said Russia does not plan to attack Europe, but Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov warned European nations against sending troops to Ukraine, which would be seen by Russia as a declaration of war."If Europe attacks Russia, it will be a completely different war, and it will be very short," he said.Meanwhile on Friday, Russia reiterated its warning to the UK that any British military facilities in Ukraine used to strike Russian territory were "legitimate targets". It reserved the right to take "necessary counter-measures" in response to the UK's "fiercely confrontational stance regarding Ukraine", referring to its supply of drones and other weapon systems to Kyiv.Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.Macron also addressed the energy situation, saying that the government had been tasked with protecting critical infrastructure and the "most sensitive" defence industry and technology sites against drone and cyberattacks.He announced that France would call a meeting of the G7 to discuss energy and raise the question of gas stocks with the European Commission."In the coming weeks, we will have a G7 meeting devoted to these energy issues, both to strengthen cooperation and to avoid unnecessary tensions between the G7 countries and our main partners," Macron said. "It will also be an opportunity to consider options for a possible release or unlocking of strategic reserves."In a domestic context, he called on candidates in next year's elections not to exploit public unease by blaming the government, but to acknowledge that fuel price inflation was the result of uncontrollable international circumstances.The hard-right opposition National Rally candidate Marine le Pen is currently leading the polls for the April-May vote to replace Macron.

schema.headline: Russian hybrid attacks against Europe intensifying, says Macron

title: Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about King Charles
description: Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?" Speaking to the BBC at h
body: Reacting to the rare statement from the Palace, Earl Spencer said: "Well, is he furious? Is he furious or is he embarrassed?" Speaking to the BBC at his Althorp estate, he added: "I've only ever had two calls on the line with Prince Charles at any stage of my life. "I was hyper alert to what he was saying and those are precisely the words that he said and I promise that to you now. Genuinely, that is what he said. I don't hear him saying he didn't say that."Pressed on whether he had evidence to back up the claim, he said he told family and friends at the time what had been said "because it was so monstrous". In response to the Palace disputing his account, Earl Spencer, who shares his first name with the King, said: "They've sort of smudged that one, haven't they? They've said that recollections may vary."When asked which Charles the public was meant to believe, he said: "I'm telling the truth."Buckingham Palace declined to give a response to Earl Spencer's fresh comments. The remarks may bring a renewed focus to the war of words between the Palace and the King's former brother-in-law.Earl Spencer's book, Swan Song: Diana, My Sister, is due to be published next week and is expected to be highly critical of the Royal Family. In further extracts published on Thursday, he claimed how the King "sounded giddily elated" when he called him after Diana's death in a car crash in Paris on 31 August 1997, alleging Charles sounded like a "lottery winner". Earl Spencer recounts being alerted to the crash by a phone call from his sister Jane in the middle of the night at his home in Cape Town, South Africa.A call from Charles was among those that followed, and he alleges: "Unlike my other callers, who were stunned, barely able to articulate their condolences and offers of help, he sounded giddily elated - like a lottery winner, I remember thinking at the time."The death of Diana, a hugely popular figure, created a volatile atmosphere in the country at the time, with the royals accused of failing to show feeling and empathy, and seeming to be out of touch with the public mood.Earl Spencer's emotional and defiant speech at her funeral added to that cloud of grievance hanging over Diana's death at the age of 36.Prince Harry has previously said that walking behind his mother's coffin aged 12 was something no child "should be asked to do".In 2017, he told the BBC he didn't "have an opinion whether that was right or wrong", but "looking back on it", he was glad to have been part of the day.The full interview with Laura Kuenssberg will be on BBC iPlayer on Sunday from 16:00 BST and on BBC One at 18:30 BST.

schema.headline: Earl Spencer defends Diana book claims about King Charles

title: Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary apologises over 'high-fare rapists' remarks
description: Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has said he is "truly sorry" for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists".He had previously refused to
body: Ryanair chief executive Michael O'Leary has said he is "truly sorry" for describing rival airlines as "high-fare rapists".He had previously refused to apologise to a rape crisis centre which criticised him for the comments.O'Leary had made the remark earlier this month while talking to journalists ahead of Ryanair's yearly meeting with shareholders.Following the comments, the Dublin Rape Crisis Centre (DRCC) wrote to him asking for an apology, in a letter seen by the BBC.O'Leary had originally said that some people were "desperate to get to Ryanair's low fares because they can't afford to fly with the high-fare rapists around Europe".He subsequently defended his choice of words when asked by a reporter from the Press Association whether the language was appropriate."British Airways, Lufthansa, and everybody else's high fares, I'll happily offend them on a regular basis," he had added.Asked whether it would offend sexual assault victims, he said rape was "a terrible crime".In a video posted on Friday, O'Leary said that, over the last ten days, he had had "conversations with family and friends, both inside and outside Ryanair"."I have come to realise however that the word that I used so carelessly has caused considerable upset and offence to a wide number of people, especially to victims and survivors."I want to apologise, sincerely and unreservedly, to those people, especially to the survivors."O'Leary described his choice of language as "careless", and said "it won't happen again"."I will try to learn from this mistake, and do better in future."Following O'Leary's first comments, the DRCC's chief executive Rachel Morrogh had written to O'Leary accusing him of trying to get a headline with his comments.She said the DRCC had received calls from rape victims who were "upset and distressed because of what you said".She offered O'Leary training on the impact of sexual violence and urged him to apologise."I can't imagine you would ever use the term so flippantly again if you truly understood [what] it was like to survive rape," she wrote.In response, O'Leary had said: "I am quite clear that no remarks of mine could possibly trivialise the heinous crime of rape."He added that as he had not "trivialised the heinous crime of rape" he would "not be issuing any apology or accepting your offer of training".It was not the first time O'Leary had offended people while talking about his business.In 2004, he reportedly called the owners of Stansted Airport "a bunch of overcharging rapists", external in a row over airport charges.He has also previously called some of his own staff "lazy bastards" and once said to passengers looking for a refund "we don't want to hear your sob stories".In June, he said the airline would "reluctantly" stop charging parents to sit next to children after a watchdog investigation was opened, but insisted its previous policy complied with laws.

schema.headline: Ryanair boss Michael O'Leary apologises over 'high-fare rapists' remarks

title: Police begin operation to move migrants from Ceuta beaches
description: Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.Officers struggl
body: Police have begun moving hundreds of migrants in Ceuta to a new tented site in the port area of the Spanish territory in north Africa.Officers struggled to contain crowds of people jostling to secure a place at the site after weeks of living on the beaches. Shots could be heard, with reports that police fired into the air.Several hundred migrants have now reached the camp, which has a capacity for 1,700 people.Most of the 72,000 migrants who breached the border from Morocco in July have returned. Ceuta's authorities have estimated that 13,000 remain in the enclave, but the Spanish central government has said it is lower.The operation began at about 07:00 local time (05:00 GMT) on Friday, with more than 3,000 migrants being transferred, according to the Spanish government-owned news agency Efe.During the process, some migrants broke through the cordon along the designated 2km (1.2 mile) route to the port. Video shows young men running in the darkness as police tried to maintain control.More than 170 police officers have been deployed, including drone technicians, Efe reported. It added that the situation was later "brought under control quickly", and the operation was able to continue.The operation is part of the government's attempt to concentrate the migrants in facilities where they can be identified and cared for while their administrative status is individually determined.The chaotic scenes will do little to dampen opposition criticism in Spain of Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, who has faced strong criticism over his handling of the crisis.Since the migrant influx, residents of the 18.5 sq km (7.2 sq miles) territory have expressed safety concerns. Some have destroyed shelters and blocked aid being supplied to the migrants.Ceuta's Mayor Juan Jesus Vivas told lawmakers in the European Parliament earlier this month that the migrants had turned Ceuta into a "pressure cooker"."The city is completely different than it was before this event, Ceutans have lost their joy and their lifestyles have been completely shaken up," the conservative mayor said.The opposition also accused Sánchez of knowing about the influx of migrants in advance. Sánchez has insisted that it was impossible to predict, but according to government documents, its intelligence services had warned of social media calls for a mass migrant crossing into Ceuta the day before the events happened.Ester Muñoz of the conservative People's Party said the government was "directly responsible for the invasion of Ceuta and for those who died".Sanchez has blamed trafficking gangs and has also said the crisis was sparked by hoaxes and rumours spread by social media.Ceuta was "a humanitarian crisis and also an administrative challenge within the city itself", the prime minister said.

schema.headline: Police begin operation to move migrants from Ceuta beaches

title: Stephanie Cole: Coronation Street and Doc Martin actress dies aged 84
description: Image source, Getty ImagesByPaul GlynnCulture reporterActress Stephanie Cole, known for roles in Tenko, Open All Hours and Coronation Street, has died
body: Image source, Getty ImagesByPaul GlynnCulture reporterActress Stephanie Cole, known for roles in Tenko, Open All Hours and Coronation Street, has died aged 84.A statement from her agent John Grant, issued on behalf of her family, confirmed the actress had been living with Alzheimer's for several years."Stephanie was an extraordinary talent whose long and distinguished career included many iconic performances in theatre and television," the statement read."She brought joy to millions through her many much-loved roles in sitcom and drama. She will also be remembered for her tireless work supporting mental health charities."Image source, Lookout Point/HBO/Aimee SpinksImage caption, Cole's credits included a role opposite Suranne Jones in Gentleman JackImage source, Gary Moyes/BBCImage caption, Cole appeared opposite David Jason once again in the 2010s reboot Still Open All HoursSolihull-born Cole, who trained at Bristol Old Vic Theatre School, after making her stage debut at the age of 17 – playing the 90-year-old medium Madame Arcati in Noel Coward's Blithe Spirit.She went on to enjoy a lengthy career that spanned TV, radio and film and was perhaps best known for playing Dr Beatrice Mason in the 1980s BBC wartime TV drama Tenko.The series chronicled the lives of British women in Singapore after the Japanese invasion and their consequent confinement in a Japanese prisoner of war camp.Cole, in her breakout role, played a doctor who struggled to look after the women's health, opposite Ann Bell and Claire Oberman.During this same period, Cole also played the moody customer Mrs Delphine Featherstone, aka "The Black Widow" in the Ronnie Barker-starring Open All Hours.She would go on to win the award for best TV comedy actress for her part as the sharp-tongued photojournalist Diana Trent in Waiting For God.But she cited her earlier performance as Muriel in Alan Bennett's monologue Soldiering On, as one of her proudest moments. The series also starred Maggie Smith and Julie Walters.Her stage highlight, by her account, was in a West End production of A Passionate Woman.Image source, ITV/ShutterstockImage caption, Cole also played Roy Cropper's mother in ITV soap Coronation Street for two years from 2011Image caption, Cole (pictured alongside co-star Ann Bell) was perhaps best known for the 1980s series TenkoCole also played the aunt of Martin Clunes's titular character in the ITV medical drama Doc Martin.Her other notable roles included Keeping Mum, and the BBC Radio 4 sitcom Cabin Pressure - alongside a fast-rising Benedict Cumberbatch - as Carolyn Knapp-Shappey."One of the joys of my character was how strong and feisty she is: she had the upper hand over the men, for the most part," she told the Guardian, external in 2018."Carolyn told it like it was and took no [rubbish]. We've all met women like her. She was very easy to put on, and I confess perhaps there's a little of her bossiness in me."She also appeared in Coronation Street as Roy Cropper's mother Sylvia Goodwin, which won her another comedy prize, in her 70s, at the 2012 British Soap Awards.Cole reprised her earlier role in the 2010s reboot Still Open All Hours, opposite David Jason, and also appeared alongside Suranne Jones in Gentleman Jack.On Halloween 2018, she also guest starred in the live episode of Reece Shearsmith and Steve Pemberton's Inside No.9, titled Dead Line.Image caption, Cole appeared opposite Ronnie Barker as the moody customer Mrs Delphine Featherstone in the 1980sImage source, PA MediaImage caption, Cole was made an OBE at Buckingham Palace in 2005The actress's stage work included Driving Miss Daisy, Noises Off and King Lear.In 2004, she returned to her debut theatre role in Blithe Spirit aged 63 when the play was revived at the West End's Savoy Theatre.She also appeared in Midsomer Murders and Doctors. Her last major TV role was appearing opposite Greg Davies in his BBC comedy series The Cleaner in 2021.Cole was married twice – first to playwright and theatrical fight director Henry Marshall, whom she divorced in 1988.A decade later, she married fellow actor Peter Birrel, 30 years after the pair first appeared together in a production of Richard II at the Bristol Old Vic.Birrel died in 2004. Cole is survived by a daughter from her first marriage, Emma Battcock.Cole was made an OBE in 2005, for her services to drama, the elderly and mental health charities.

schema.headline: Stephanie Cole: Coronation Street and Doc Martin actress dies aged 84

title: MI5 accepts it gave evidence based on lies in neo-Nazi spy case
description: He said "MI5 accepts without reservation" the findings of a damning report which concluded that it gave evidence based on "lies" about having kept to
body: He said "MI5 accepts without reservation" the findings of a damning report which concluded that it gave evidence based on "lies" about having kept to its core secrecy policy - known as 'neither confirm nor deny' (NCND) - about the agent status of the neo-Nazi informant.The security service claimed it had maintained NCND and, consequently, the courts allowed it to keep information secret from a woman who was abused by him.But what MI5 said was untrue. The security service had in fact disclosed the man's agent status in phone calls to me, as it tried to persuade me not to investigate him in 2020.A panel of three senior judges - England and Wales' most senior judge, Lady Chief Justice Baroness Sue Carr, President of the King's Bench Division Dame Victoria Sharp and Mr Justice Chamberlain - is considering what action to take over the false evidence.In particular, it will decide whether to initiate contempt of court proceedings against certain MI5 officers or MI5 itself. Any such move would be unprecedented.The report, by then-deputy investigatory powers commissioner Sir John Goldring, found that one senior MI5 spy - known as Officer 2 - lied repeatedly, while another - Officer 3 - misled his own colleagues and lied about what he was told. He also found there were "serious and systemic failures in MI5's conduct" throughout the case.Otty said MI5 "fully accepts and acknowledges the gravity of the issues raised" in the report, published in July, and they must never happen again.He added that MI5 had committed to a major programme of reform under the leadership of director general Sir Ken McCallum.Otty argued against contempt proceedings being brought, saying it would not be in the public interest given Sir John's detailed investigation, MI5's apologies, and its commitment to a programme of reform.He said Officer 2 had resigned from the service and that Officer 3 had been suspended and was facing disciplinary proceedings, which could lead to his dismissal.Lawyers for both officers also argued against launching contempt proceedings.Matthew Butt KC, for Officer 2, said the officer accepted that his conduct had fallen "below the standard expected of him", for which he apologised and expressed regret. But he said he denied acting dishonestly or having interfered with the administration of justice, and did not accept the report's findings.Aaron Watkins apologised on behalf of Officer 3 and accepted his conduct "undoubtably" contributed to the courts and parties involved being misled, but denied it had been the result of dishonesty.He said the evidence presented by Sir John fell short of the threshold for contempt of court, and said such proceedings would not be in the public interest because there had already been a thorough investigation.Meanwhile, lawyers for the BBC said the corporation considered the threshold had been met and said there was a "very clear public interest" in doing so.Jude Bunting KC said providing false evidence was "a particularly serious affront to the administration of justice" and noted that while MI5 now offered a sincere apology to the court, its response when the lies were first exposed was "not consistent with transparency or responsibility".At the conclusion of the hearing, the Lady Chief Justice said it had been a "serious day addressing serious matters".She said a judgment will be issued at a later date.The case centres around the foreign neo-Nazi misogynist - an MI5 informant known as Agent X who used his security service role as a tool of abuse.He coercively controlled his partner, known by the alias Beth, and attacked her with a machete. MI5 then helped him go abroad to continue intelligence work while under police investigation.The government took the BBC to court in 2022 in a failed attempt to block its investigation into X, but won him legal anonymity. Beth then sued MI5 at the Investigatory Powers Tribunal, and in 2024 she sought a review of a ruling at the High Court.Arguing for secrecy in all three courts, the security service told judges that it had always stuck to its core secrecy policy and never told anyone whether X was an agent, including me. The courts were told this in a sworn statement from a senior officer, a deputy director called Witness A.The courts accepted MI5's arguments. This meant Beth and everyone else was banned from ever officially being told X was an agent and denied access to the key evidence. She was left at a serious disadvantage and may have lost the case.Officer 2 had tried to cover up for the man, falsely saying he was not an abusive misogynist nor a real extremist.Following the court decision in late 2024, I challenged MI5 and said they had lied to the courts. MI5 aggressively maintained its position that its NCND policy had been maintained until I produced evidence proving it was untrue, including a recording of one of the calls with Officer 2.Because of the BBC's revelations, two official inquiries took place which absolved MI5 and its officers of deliberate wrongdoing, claiming the false evidence was down to mistakes and poor memories.But, in July 2025, a panel of senior High Court judges ruled that the investigations carried out by MI5 suffered from "serious procedural deficiencies" and that "we cannot rely on their conclusions".Sir John's investigation was ordered by the prime minister in September 2025 after MI5's explanations about what happened were rejected as deficient and unreliable.Charlotte Kilroy KC, for Beth, said contempt proceedings should be brought against Officers 2 and 3, as well as the Director General of MI5 Sir Ken McCallum in his capacity as the person with corporate responsibility for the organisation.In written submissions, she said the false evidence "did not emanate from one individual, or a "bad apple'" and was "sustained and long-lasting".She added: "There have been repeated efforts to prevent the truth emerging. The reality of the dishonesty and false evidence that has taken place has only emerged because MI5 was faced with incontrovertible proof of its wrongdoing."She told the court that the "function" of the Goldring report was to allow it to consider whether to bring contempt proceedings, meaning the report was never meant to be the final word."Contempt proceedings are essential", she said.

schema.headline: MI5 accepts it gave evidence based on lies in neo-Nazi spy case

title: Billionaire Manchester United owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe says he has lost confidence in UK
description: One of Britain's richest people, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, says he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide".The founder of pet
body: One of Britain's richest people, Sir Jim Ratcliffe, says he has lost confidence in the UK, describing the country as "on the slide".The founder of petrochemical giant Ineos, who also owns a large stake in Manchester United, said the UK was in decline due to a combination of high taxes and high immigration.He told the BBC failing to invest further in North Sea oil and gas amounted to "insanity" and warned gas storage was so low that the UK could "run out of gas" if there was a cold snap this winter.In response to the billionaire's criticism, the government said it was working to deliver growth and that business investment had increased in the last two years.A spokesperson said they did not foresee any problems with gas supply: "We have a diverse energy mix and are confident in our security of supply."Sir Jim, whose wealth is estimated to be around £15bn, has prompted controversy in the past with his comments on immigration. He was a supporter of Brexit but has been a tax resident in Monaco since 2020.The businessman's UK exit has been followed by other high-profile billionaires, including steel tycoon Lakshmi Mittal and most recently hedge-fund boss Chris Rokos.Sir Jim said the politics of envy was driving people away from the UK."In America they applaud people who create wealth," he said. "Unfortunately the UK has got a bit of a green eye towards wealth at the moment."He said for him to return to the UK "things would have to get better".Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said he will take a "pragmatic approach" to oil and gas, but one of the biggest decisions facing the government, whether to give the go-ahead to further development of the oil and gas fields at Rosebank and Jackdaw, is still waiting to be resolved.Sir Jim criticised the hesitation and suggested high taxes on North Sea operators were threatening the sector's viability. Tax on energy company profits is being reformed, but won't be fully implemented until 2030.Ineos operates the Forties pipeline which transports about 30% of the UK's North Sea oil."You would expect [the government] to exploit our natural resources and we're clearly not doing that. We're shutting it down. "If you tax everybody to death, they're all going to leave. And that's what's happening."Recent climate data combined with record heatwaves have given weight to the argument against further exploitation of fossil fuels. However, political pressure has grown on the government to proceed with Rosebank and Jackdaw to support UK jobs, tax revenues and boost energy security.Sir Jim backed those calls, saying it was "absurd" to import more energy than necessary.The government spokesperson said that oil and gas would play an important role in the UK "for decades to come", but they added: "The transition to homegrown clean power is the only way to deliver energy and financial security for families and businesses."Sir Jim warned that low gas storage levels in Europe posed a risk to the UK in the months ahead."If we have a really sharp cold spell, then there is conceivably the possibility that we'll run out of gas and have to switch industry off... our storage is not full," he said.The UK does not typically store a great deal of gas, relying instead on LNG (liquidfied natural gas) and gas imports from Europe. Energy specialist consultancy Cornwall Insight said that current gas storage levels in the EU were at about 69%, when typically they would be at 85% at this time of the year. However, Adam Bell of consultancy Stonehaven, said supplies were unlikely to run short."We are down compared to where we normally would be but not what I'd regard as catastrophic," he said."The physical risk of running out of gas is relatively low, especially if Jackdaw gets the go ahead."He said the main source of uncertainty was policy in the US, which supplies LNG to the UK.Sir Jim was speaking in Denmark at the launch of the EU's first carbon capture and storage system (CCS). Ineos has invested in the scheme which is being subsidised by the Danish government and the EU. He said he had hoped to develop CCS in the UK but there had not been enough  government support.The Department for Energy Security and Net Zero (DESNZ) said the government had committed £21.7bn for CCS projects over 25 years, however, no projects are yet operational in the UK. At the project in Esbjerg in the south west of Denmark, carbon captured from around the country arrives in huge zeppelin-like tanks before being pumped into a ship called Carbon Destroyer 1. It is then pumped into a depleted oil field nearly 200 miles off shore.Critics say CCS is expensive, money that could be better used to invest in renewables rather than supporting continued fossil fuel use.Sir Jim's critique of the UK is not limited to energy and tax policy. He said the country had at one time been "a fantastic place"."We had the greatest empire in the world. We were a great people. We won two world wars," he said. But he said immigration and welfare spending were both currently too high and that politicians had proved reluctant to tackle either."Nobody's tough enough to deal with the immigration problem. Nobody's tough enough to deal with the benefits problem. But somebody needs to do it," he said.Earlier this year he caused controversy by saying the UK had been "colonised by immigrants".He later offered an apology for "offending some people".You can listen to the full interview here on the Big Boss Interview podcast with Simon Jack.

schema.headline: Billionaire Manchester United owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe says he has lost confidence in UK

title: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents
description: A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residentsImage source, BBC News UkraineImage caption, Daria l
body: A four-minute warning isn't enough: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residentsImage source, BBC News UkraineImage caption, Daria left her apartment in Kyiv this summer after Russia's attacks on the city intensifiedByDiana Kuryshko and Victoria KalimbetBBC News UkrainianFor much of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Daria was not afraid of the shelling.Even on nights of heavy bombardment, the 27-year-old could sleep through the explosions in her apartment in Kyiv. Like many Ukrainians, she relied on the "two-wall rule": staying safe by keeping two walls between herself and the outside world.But this year that has changed.In recent months, Russia has scaled up the intensity and frequency of its attacks against the Ukrainian capital. In the first 10 days of July alone, the Russians launched dozens of ballistic missiles in three major attacks, killing nearly 60 civilians, according to official figures. Similar large scale attacks took place in August and September. A BBC Verify analysis of government figures found Kyiv is now suffering more daily air raid alerts than at any time since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022.It was during an attack one night in May that Daria realised she no longer felt safe in her home.She and her boyfriend were in the corridor of their ninth-floor apartment, watching a boxing match, as explosions went off around them, the blast waves causing the windows to repeatedly slam open and shut.When the fight ended, "there was no longer anything to distract me," Daria says. "That's when I realised I was really scared."At first, she thought she would start using a nearby bomb shelter during attacks.But in June, when a young mother was killed running to a shelter in Kyiv, Daria decided she needed to leave the city altogether. She returned to her family's country house, 30km (18.6 miles) away in Romankiv, and now spends a total of four hours a day commuting to and from Kyiv, where she works in the defence sector.Image source, Ukraine State Emergency ServiceImage caption, A photo from the State Emergency Service shows the impact of a Russian strike in JulyDaria's experience is far from unique.Residents in Kyiv who say they had got used to Russia's missile and drone strikes have told the BBC World Service the renewed intensity of the attacks is making them rethink how they live their lives.Previously, Ukraine's air-defence network and military intelligence gave residents a degree of predictability. Large-scale attacks could often be detected in advance, allowing people to spend the night in shelters, leave the city or take other precautions. But since the summer, Russia has changed its tactics.It has relied less on aircraft, whose movements can be spotted ahead of time, and more on ballistic missiles that travel at tremendous speed and provide little warning. Air-raid alerts sometimes begin only moments before impact, or even simultaneously with the first explosions. Daria can see her nearest shelter from the window of her apartment, which she still rents. Even so, it takes around 10 minutes to reach it. During a ballistic attack, she might have just four minutes' warning or less, she says.She decided to leave Kyiv in June after holidaying abroad this summer and seeing people living "normal" lives. Since then, she has only spent one night in Kyiv.Image caption, Ballistic missiles are difficult to detect in advanceYet, for many, leaving is not an option.Sixty-two-year-old Olha Vlasova lives on the seventh floor of a high-rise apartment block with her 98-year-old mother, Nadia Tsybina.Despite her age, Nadia remains intensely engaged with the world. From her bed she follows events in Ukraine and abroad, discussing everything from US President Donald Trump's policies, to anti-corruption protests in Kyiv, and the Epstein files.She's also learned that she can often tell, simply by listening, whether a Russian missile or drone has been intercepted or has reached its target.This summer, she says she has heard fewer interceptions."It's upsetting when there's nothing to shoot them down with," Nadia says. "I can hear them firing with whatever they've got, rifles, machine guns."Image source, BBC News UkraineImage caption, Nadia, 98, continues to follow world events closely from her bedImage source, BBC News UkraineImage caption, Olha has taken to placing a mattress by the window to protect her and her mother from flying glassWith Nadia confined to her bed, she and Olha cannot go to a shelter, however serious an attack is. Instead, as soon as an air-raid siren sounds, Olha covers her mother with a blanket, pushes a mattress into their window frame, and then hides in a wardrobe which puts two walls between her and outside.Nadia places a pillow over her head to protect her face from flying glass.Once in her wardrobe, Olha will often stay awake watching the news all night."They come in, they bomb us," Nadia says. "You haven't even had time to fall asleep, and there's another alert. They come again, they shoot them down again. And it goes on all night. "People don't sleep, and then they walk around like zombies."Image source, Global Images Ukraine via Getty ImagesImage caption, The new academic year in Kyiv began with many students attending classes in shelters as an air raid alert was in effect in the morningAn increase in daytime attacks means life in Kyiv is now interrupted by air raid sirens day and night. At the beginning of September, when children returned to school after the summer break, there were dozens of air raid alerts, followed by explosions and fires. According to Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko, two children were injured in attacks on 31 August.As a result, many children stayed at home, while others spent hours in the basements of schools and kindergartens.Image source, ReutersImage caption, Commuters in Kyiv have become accustomed to long wait times as the metro is disrupted.When the sirens sound, it also affects businesses and transport. Shopping centres close and above-ground metro stations suspend operations, often severing public transport links between Kyiv's Left and Right Banks, on either side of the Dnieper River, for hours at a time.New metro operating rules during air raid alerts are being introduced in an attempt to improve the situation.For Olha, it has meant seeing less of her eight-year-old granddaughter, who lives on the other side of the city. She knows if her granddaughter comes to visit, she risks struggling to return home. When metro services stop running, expensive cab journeys are Olha's only option. Crossing the river can cost as much as 1,000 hryvnias ($22, £16.6), she says, just under one-eighth of Ukraine's monthly minimum wage.The experience has left her frustrated with what she sees as hesitation by some of Ukraine's foreign partners to provide additional air-defence missiles. President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly appealed to allies for additional air-defence systems and interceptor missiles."They [Ukraine's allies] wait, thinking: 'What if we get attacked?'" Olha says. "It's like refusing to give medicine to a cancer patient because you're saying, 'What if I get sick one day?' Well, maybe you won't. Give it away before it expires."Image source, Natalia BushkovskaImage caption, Neither Natalia nor her daughter can sleep through the nightly attacksIn another part of the city, mother-of-two Natalia Bushkovska each night rehearses three different plans. Plan A is to spread bedding in the hallway behind two interior walls; Plan B is to move the family into the building's shared corridor; and Plan C is to head for the basement.Even there, she admits, she does not feel entirely safe."I keep a backpack with essential items," says Natalia, 37. "There's a tourniquet for severe bleeding. I also keep a whistle, just in case. "If the worst happens, rescuers will be able to find us under the rubble."Her nine-year-old daughter has her own emergency bag containing toys, lip balm and a tourniquet. Like her 12-year-old brother, she learned how to use a tourniquet through first-aid training. Natalia says the constant attacks are exhausting. While her son often sleeps through them, she and her daughter wake up almost every time."Because of the attacks, I don't get enough sleep," she says. "Now, in the fifth year of the war, I find it increasingly difficult to bounce back after nights like these."The growing intensity of the strikes, she says, is taking a psychological toll across the city."People are exhausted. They don't have enough time to recover."On Thursday 17 September, Russia launched a ballistic missile attack on Kyiv. According to Mayor Vitali Klitschko, 20 people were injured in the attack. Among the wounded were two children, aged 10 and 12.Additional reporting by Janet Ball

schema.headline: Russia's new relentless missile tactics exhaust Kyiv residents

title: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I'm like my character in Sense and Sensibility
description: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I try and bury my emotion when it comes to loveImage source, Getty ImagesByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentDaisy Edgar-Jones has bee
body: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I try and bury my emotion when it comes to loveImage source, Getty ImagesByNoor NanjiCulture correspondentDaisy Edgar-Jones has been well cast in her new film.She plays Elinor, the rational elder sister in Sense and Sensibility, opposite the younger, more romantic sister Marianne.Speaking to the BBC, Edgar-Jones says that in her personal life, she really is like her character."When it comes to love, I think I am very much more Elinor in every sort of way," she says."I definitely lead a lot with my head and try and push aside, bury my emotion."But she notes that one of the joys of the film is seeing Elinor learn to enjoy a "wilder, passionate side" of herself. "And I feel like I learnt to do that too," she says.Best known for starring in hit TV series Normal People with Paul Mescal, Edgar-Jones, 28, is now taking on a lead role in the latest adaptation of Jane Austen's book.Ahead of its release, she’s been talking to me about whether we really need another Sense and Sensibility film (spoiler: yes. “The more the merrier, in my opinion.”)She also told me why young people today can still see themselves in Jane Austen's stories - and gave me her take on whether her friend and former co-star Mescal should be the next James Bond. Image source, Alex Bailey / 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLCImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Esmé Creed-Miles in a scene from Sense and SensibilityThe new film, directed by Georgia Oakley, follows the Dashwood sisters as they navigate their way through love, loss and societal expectations, following the death of their father.It's a classic adaptation of Austen's novel, rather than a more contemporary take.When I meet Edgar-Jones at a hotel in central London, I ask her whether there was ever a temptation to make it more "2026"."It does feel very much like it's honouring the period," she agrees, "but I think there's a freshness to the filmmaking that I think is really beautiful".She is starring alongside Esmé Creed-Miles, 26, who plays her sister Marianne.Together, the two sisters' different approaches to life are characterised as "sense" (Elinor) and "sensibility" (Marianne).Creed-Miles is also well cast, it seems. "I'm more like Marianne [than Elinor], yeah, which is annoying sometimes," she laughs.Image source, Alex Bailey / 2026 FOCUS FEATURES LLCImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones stars as Elinor in Sense and SensibilitySense and Sensibility has been adapted for screen countless times before - including the hit 1995 film starring Emma Thompson and Kate Winslet.Edgar-Jones loves that version (“one of my favourite films of all time”) but also feels there's room to tell Austen’s classic tale again."Her stories are something that fascinate us still today,” she says.It was also easy for her and Creed-Mills to build the sisterly rapport on screen, as they previously worked together as teenagers on the 2018 film Pond Life.“We had a real laugh," Creed-Mills says of their time on that film. "We would have sleepovers every night and watch Love Island."For Edgar-Jones, the theme of sisterhood is something that stuck with her from Sense and Sensibility - despite her being an only child in real life.“I've heard a lot of people say that after watching the film, it either makes them want a sister or to ring up their sister and say like, ‘Hey, I love you,’ and I think that's really special. It's the part of the film I'm most proud of.”Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Esmé Creed-Miles and Daisy Edgar-Jones play two sisters in Sense & SensibilityJane Austen seems to be everywhere right now.Last year marked the 250th anniversary of her birth and, in recent years, we've enjoyed two BBC TV series, Miss Austen and The Other Bennet Sister, the West End's Clueless musical (based on the cult 90s teen film adaptation of Emma), and Ava Pickett's modern stage adaptation of Emma.There's also a new adaptation of Pride and Prejudice written by Dolly Alderton and starring Emma Corrin coming to Netflix.For Edgar-Jones, the themes in Austen's books are just as revelant today."She has an incredible way of articulating the female experience," she says."Her ruminations on love, on romance, on sisterly love, on family dynamics, on interpersonal social dynamics - she's such a talent."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones takes a selfie with a fan at the world premiere for Sense and Sensibility in London earlier this weekAusten also wrote about the sort of dating behaviour that people complain about on TikTok (like situationships and ghosting), before terms like that had even been invented. Does that help Gen Z audiences relate to her, I ask?"Well, massively," replies Edgar-Jones."We still have the same human heart as we did 200 years ago. Our capacity to love and feel heartbreak, and that early first love feeling, is something that we all experience in various ways."And so yes, I think definitely the trials and tribulations of the two women [Elinor and Marianne] as they navigate life, love and all that becomes as you grow up, definitely is so relatable to all generations.""These women are very relatable," agrees Creed-Mills."I don't know if seeing a movie is going to fix everything, but it might make you feel a little bit less alone in some of the things you're feeling."Image source, Getty ImagesImage caption, Daisy Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal's breakout roles were in Normal People, which came out in 2020Edgar-Jones shot to fame during the pandemic with her role in Normal People.Based on Sally Rooney's novel, the BBC Three drama charted the on-off relationship of teenagers Marianne and Connell, played by Edgar-Jones and Paul Mescal.The pair have remained close (a few years ago, Edgar-Jones told me Mescal was "one of my all-time best friends") - and both are now successful actors. Edgar-Jones has since starred in Twisters and Where The Crawdads Sing, while Mescal was in Gladiator II, Hamnet and will be in the Beatles films.Recently, Page Six claimed Mescal was on the audition list to be the next James Bond, external.So, is he really in the running? Edgar-Jones didn’t give too much away.“I don’t know, but I think there’s nothing Paul can’t do,” she says.“So I would be there. Wow, that’s cool.”Sense and Sensibility is out in UK cinemas on 25 September.

schema.headline: Daisy Edgar-Jones: I'm like my character in Sense and Sensibility

title: Athlos London: Keely Hodgkinson powers to victory in speed suit at all-female event
description: Figure caption, 'Speed meeting style' - Hogkinson charges ahead to win Athlos 800mByHarry PooleBBC Sport journalistUpdated 3 hours agoKeely Hodgkinson
body: Figure caption, 'Speed meeting style' - Hogkinson charges ahead to win Athlos 800mByHarry PooleBBC Sport journalistUpdated 3 hours agoKeely Hodgkinson powered to victory in a custom-made full-body speed suit before being presented with a Tiffany & Co crown as Athlos made its London debut.Hodgkinson was greeted by loud cheers as she emerged on to a stage and revealed the all-black aerodynamic outfit at the third staging of the all-female athletics meet.The 24-year-old ensured she ended a mixed year with a dominant 800m victory in front of a sellout home crowd at StoneX Stadium, bursting clear on the back straight and crossing the line in one minute 56.40 seconds.Speaking about the outfit, Hodgkinson told BBC Sport: "This has been like a year in the making. It's a mixture of fashion and speed and science all coming together for maybe the future of athletics."It was a real honour for them to choose me to put this out first. We weren't sure when we were going to wear it."But an all-women's event that's all about the glitz and the glamour and putting eyes on women, a bit of a moment, I think was the perfect way to finish the season."Created by Alexis Ohanian, Reddit co-founder and husband of tennis' 23-time Grand Slam singles champion Serena Williams, Athlos was staging a meet for the first time outside of New York.In addition to the silver Tiffany crown awarded to winners instead of medals, a top prize of $65,000 (£48,500) was on offer in each event.The single-night meet included seven disciplines, each featuring six athletes, with money on offer for each position from a total event prize pot of $1.05m (£790,500).American sprint stars Gabby Thomas and Sha'Carri Richardson were among the champions amid a party atmosphere which featured a live track-side DJ.Hodgkinson ends mixed year with crown and a smileFigure caption, Hodgkinson shows off her dance moves at AthlosThe athletes had arrived on a red carpet in north London but Hodgkinson saved her starring moment for the main event.The eye-catching speed suit, reminiscent of that worn by Cathy Freeman in winning Olympic 400m gold in 2000, featured an open back and a hood with a ponytail opening - the latter, she said, was non-negotiable - while colour-changing 3D-printed nodes reduced drag in key areas.Paired with dark sunglasses and Nike's latest carbon-plated spikes, it helped Hodgkinson achieve her first victory since the London Diamond League in July. It has been a year of record-breaking highs and frustrating setbacks for the Olympic champion.An indoor season in which she landed her first world 800m title and smashed a 24-year world record heightened expectations that she would take down the sport's longest-standing mark outdoors.But a nasty fall suffered on a post-session cool down run in July, and a recurrence of the hamstring injury which kept her out of action for much of 2025 at the European Championships, conspired to hinder her progress.While still improving her British record this summer, Hodgkinson finished second to breakout Swiss star Audrey Werro at both the European Championships and inaugural World Athletics Ultimate Championship.However, with Swiss athlete Valentina Rosamilia finishing more than two seconds behind, she ended the season with a smile on her face and a crown on her head as she danced on stage with the night's other winners.Figure caption, Dramatic sprint finish - Hunter Bell second in Athlos mileTraining partner Georgia Hunter Bell was pipped to victory in the mile by Poland's Klaudia Kazimierska.Diamond League champion Kazimierska, who denied Hunter Bell in her bid to win a fourth major title of 2026 at last week's World Athletics Ultimate Championship, squeezed past on the inside to edge the Briton in four minutes 19.43 seconds.That close finish left Ohanian in disbelief as he watched trackside alongside tennis great Williams and their children, with famous athletes and celebrities also present.Former world champion Richardson stormed to victory in the 100m in 10.80 seconds, as Britons Imani-Lara Lansiquot (11.35) and Daryll Neita (11.36) placed fourth and fifth respectively.Olympic 200m champion Thomas took victory in the final race of the night, winning the 200m in 22.13 seconds, while Dominican Olympic champion Marileidy Paulino overhauled Norway's Henriette Jaeger to win the 400m in 48.73 seconds.There were also wins for Americans Alaysha Johnson in the 100m hurdles and Alyssa Jones in the long jump.What is Athlos and is it here to stay?Figure caption, What is the athletics event Athlos?Ohanian has been clear about his eventual intention to make Athlos a global season-long league.Athlos was supposed to expand to a two-day event in 2026, but the New York meeting scheduled for 2 October was cancelled following consultation with the athletes at the end of a long season.Instead, Ohanian now hopes to align Athlos within the global athletics calendar from next year. How that will work remains to be seen. The Diamond League, athletics' premier season-long series, runs from May until September, while the introduction of the Ultimate Championship - joining the Olympics and the World Championships on the calendar - means every season will now feature a global competition of some description.American Masai Russell, who broke the 100m hurdles world record last month, was among the late Athlos withdrawals following last week's Ultimate, organised by the sport's governing body and offering record prize pot of $10m.After a week in which countless female athletes denounced a controversial sports betting company advertisement featuring actress Sydney Sweeney, Ohanian said he wanted Friday's event to put the attention back on the "actual athletes".It achieved just that, with some of the world's top female athletes going head-to-head in competitive events while also being allowed the space to express their personalities.Ohanian is determined to bridge a perceived disconnect between the attention on the sport at each Olympic Games compared to the rest of the calendar in those four-year cycles.The 43-year-old set up the Angel City FC women's football club in Los Angeles six years ago after leaving Reddit, and purchased a 10% stake in Women's Super League team Chelsea in 2025.At Athlos, the athletes who have competed in its early events were offered equity in the league, the idea being that they will be rewarded if it is successful."I would have loved to have had this when I was younger. Hopefully the youngsters can see this and have their time one day," Hodgkinson said.While some have criticised the exclusion of men's events, Ohanian said an initial focus on female athletes was a business decision and he has identified the 2028 edition, around the Los Angeles Olympics, an opportunity to expand in that regard.Figure caption, Quick-fire questions on the Athlos red carpetAthlos lived up to hypeBySports News CorrespondentAthlos set out to be different, and it definitely felt that. There was as much showbusiness as there was sport - this was all about the "event".Athletes arrived on bespoke London buses and walked the red carpet before their event. Several of the athletes said they enjoyed having the spotlight on them and being able to combine their sport with fashion and many will now be part of London Fashion Week.Georgia Hunter Bell emerged from a melee of screaming children telling her she was their idol onto the red carpet and said she felt "valued".It was certainly noisy, and the resident DJ meant at times it felt more like you were in a club than an athletics meet. But the athletes and fans seemed to buy into the vibe.One man told me he had been to 27 world championships and five Olympics and wasn't sure he'd enjoy Athlos, but loved it. A woman whose daughter is part of the athletics club who train at StoneX Stadium said she thought it was "remarkable" and "inspirational".There will be learnings from this first trip to London, but as a starting point, it felt like it lived up to its hype.Figure caption, Athlos founder Ohanian on Hodgkinson's 'star power'

schema.headline: Athlos London: Keely Hodgkinson powers to victory in speed suit at all-female event

title: An American found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and hopes others do too
description: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the sameFigure caption, "It was very serendipitous" - Mary and Jason on findin
body: I found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and I want others to do the sameFigure caption, "It was very serendipitous" - Mary and Jason on finding love in IrelandBySheila FlynnSenior US ReporterMary Timby was fed up with dating apps when she booked a trip to Ireland on a whim last summer - from the comfort of her Colorado couch.The spur-of-the-moment trip was unlike her: Timby, 39, is a self-described "total planner". But she'd always wanted to visit Ireland, and she found herself exhausted by the local dating scene while navigating a career transition. And then she remembered a few throwaway lines from a comedy series about a matchmaking festival in Ireland.So she looked it up - and not only was the Lisdoonvarna Matchmaking Festival real, it was also taking place during the entire month of September, when she was scheduled to visit.Now, a little more than a year later, Timby is reaping the benefits of that uncharacteristic last-minute decision: She's become a viral star. She's found love with an Irishman she met at a pub called The Matchmaker. And she's even started a new business venture - bringing others to Lisdoonvarna who hope to follow in her footsteps.Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, Timby and Jason Mangan, 38, from County Clare, Ireland, are pursuing a transatlantic romance"It's really about enjoying County Clare, enjoying the festival, and, if you meet someone, you do - and that's what happened with us," says Timby, smiling at her partner, Jason Mangan, sitting beside her.They're speaking from the windswept coastal cottage they rented together for the summer in his native County Clare - about 20 miles (32 km) southwest of Lisdoonvarna, the site of their first fortuitous meeting.'Mary, your video is going viral'From the outset, Timby's inaugural Ireland trip seemed to take on a life of its own.She filmed a short video on the plane before her flight took off, telling her approximately 300 TikTok followers that she was heading on an off-the-cuff trip to an Irish matchmaking festival - and didn't "know what's going to happen".Timby then "turned my phone on airplane mode, then spent about eight hours on the flight (and) woke up at Shannon Airport," she says.When she turned on her phone, "it was blowing up".A group of friends had texted her. "They said, 'Mary, your video is going viral,'" she says. "I didn't even have notifications on for social media."She rented a manual transmission car - horrified to find the gear stick on the left side of the driver's seat - and set off through County Clare to her accommodation at an Irish family's home. Then she headed to Lisdoonvarna, where she saw firsthand that the festival is a whole-town, month-long celebration of conversation and dancing, rather than a line of singles waiting to be set up by a sage local matchmaker.Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, Colorado woman Mary Timby, 39, visited Ireland's Aran Islands with her new beauThat's changed since the festival's origins 170 years ago, when bachelor farmers and moneyed visitors would flock to the spa town of Lisdoonvarna to bathe in its mineral-rich waters and socialise. Generations of matchmakers would ply their trade to set up successful marriages, and word spread. Now, while the town's year-round residents number fewer than 1,000, that number swells up to 80,000 each September as revellers descend upon Lisdoonvarna from around the world.Third-generation matchmaker Willie Daly still holds court at his nearby home and at festival events, and Timby even visited him during her trip - when he put her on the phone to random men whose accents she struggled to understand.But the real magic of contemporary Lisdoonvarna lies in the town's overflowing streets and pubs - as Timby soon found out.Her first night in town was "a little slow," she admits - and Timby was tired and jet-lagged. She retired to her room and spent the next day sightseeing, but the Irish woman running her accommodation convinced her to try Lisdoonvarna again that night."My AirBnB host said, 'You should go back tonight, because I heard that the younger folks come out at night,'" laughs Timby.So she did - and found herself dancing and drinking pints at The Matchmaker Bar in the centre of town. That's when a "handsome Irishman" approached her.'Conversation just flowed'"I went over and introduced myself, and... conversation just flowed," says Mangan, 38, from Ennis, County Clare, about 22 miles southeast of Lisdoonvarna. He'd been to the festival before and was well-acquainted with its cultural significance, remembering his grandparents making the journey decades earlier for the dancing."Unfortunately, I didn't have much time on my hands, because I was turning back to Ennis," says Mangan, designated driver that night for a group of friends. "So I got her name, and I said, 'Oh, sure, I might see you around.'"It was a very short interaction, to be honest with you."Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, The couple first met at Lisdoonvarna's Matchmaker Bar during the annual festivalHe didn't leave it at that, though; Mangan found Timby on Instagram and followed up with a message inviting her out."It was short and sweet, and it was really genuine, too," says Timby - and she took him up on the offer.What followed was a series of whirlwind dates - lunches, dinners, sightseeing and shopping trips. Timby extended her time in Ireland and documented much of it for her newfound following - but she didn't reveal anything about her new beau. They wanted to save the burgeoning romance for themselves.When Timby eventually had to fly home, there were "tears at the airport" - but they decided to keep the relationship going."It was very tough to say goodbye," Timby says. "It was very tough to start a long-distance relationship, but it ended up being a really good opportunity for us to sort of slow things down a bit."They kept talking daily, Mangan impatiently waiting for Timby to wake up seven hours behind him in Colorado. She flew back to Ireland again, then he made his first trip to America for Thanksgiving 2025. Timby returned to Ireland at Christmas and met his family, and after that, they decided to make her boyfriend's big social media reveal."We thought, this is something we already know we want to invest in... we were ready to share," Timby says. "So New Year's Eve, we shared a photo of him, and people were just over-the-moon excited."The pair watched their following grow, drawing interest from Irish cafes and tourist destinations to the local Gaelic sports club in Colorado. Their story also caught the attention of Lisdoonvarna locals, who approached Timby - a communications consultant - about being an ambassador for the festival."So I said: Sign me up," Timby laughs. "I love the festival. It brought me Jay."Image source, Mary TimbyImage caption, Mangan has made repeated trips to Colorado since their 2025 meeting in IrelandTimby's been inundated with messages from lovelorn followers hoping to replicate her matchmaking success."I heard from many of my followers... groups of people wanting to go to the festival but not having anyone to go with" or "not knowing what to do," Timby says. "I really listened to that, and I also wanted to be mindful of the fact that I love Ireland."I'm so excited to showcase County Clare and all the amazing things that the west coast of Ireland has, but I'm also not a tour operator."So she partnered with a company called Met Through Friends, which organises and encourages real-life meetups for people looking for love. They released an interest form for a trip, expecting "80 to 100 responses." They received 560.The first group of eight will make the trip later this month, with Timby's Irish boyfriend consulting on the itinerary."You can go on all these apps, swipe left, swipe right, but it's not actually going out and making a connection with someone and experiencing a small little town in Ireland, experiencing the culture," says Mangan."It's a once-in-a-lifetime experience... you never know."Timby, smiling at her boyfriend of one year, agrees."I echo everything Jay just said," she says. "Put your phone down and put yourselves out there, and good things will come."

schema.headline: An American found love at an Irish matchmaking festival - and hopes others do too

title: Earl Spencer's Diana book opens old wounds royals would rather forget
description: At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Sp
body: At issue is Earl Spencer's account of a conversation with the then Prince Charles after the death of Diana, with the prince accused of telling Earl Spencer: "We'll forget her soon enough."He is accused of sounding "giddily elated" and like a "lottery winner" after the news of her death.Buckingham Palace hit back with a response, which although dressed in courtier-like politeness, was essentially saying the conversation had never happened like that.The King was said to be "mindful that the pain of fraternal grief can cloud reason, affect judgment and colour memory in ways that others do not recognise".Anyone who has lost someone knows how feelings can run high, people can hear different things about the same conversations - and families can fall out, or come together, in the wake of a death.Psychotherapist Nick Hatter says he doesn't have a view on which version of events is correct, but he says that during traumatic events memories can be "distorted". A phone call doesn't have any of the visual clues or body language to give a fuller picture, he adds.Hatter says there can be very different and unpredictable responses to grief, including a condition known as "bereavement mania" where someone can seem inappropriately hyper or even euphoric after the loss of a loved one.The first opinion poll on who to believe has been published by YouGov - and it suggests a very split view, with 31% believing Earl Spencer's allegations, 36% suspecting it's not true and 33% saying they don't know.Low thinks the book is unlikely to change many opinions, as "people have settled into their camps about how they regard Charles, how they look back on the Diana years".There could also be a feeling that it's "tawdry" to rake up these claims so many years later, he says.That's echoed by historian and author Sir Anthony Seldon who says Earl Spencer showed great courage at the time of Diana's funeral, but says his memoir is a "sad and unnecessary publication".Royal commentator Richard Palmer says the book threatens to take the royals back to the difficult days of 1997."This book and the run-up to next year's 30th anniversary of Diana's death threaten to undermine the Royal Household's three decades of work to rehabilitate Charles and Camilla's image," he says.

schema.headline: Earl Spencer's Diana book opens old wounds royals would rather forget

title: Is it cool to wear M&S clothes now?
description: Image source, Carlo Paloni/Getty ImagesImage caption, M&S show during London Fashion Week September 2026ByAnnabel RackhamCulture reporter"I'm the firs
body: Image source, Carlo Paloni/Getty ImagesImage caption, M&S show during London Fashion Week September 2026ByAnnabel RackhamCulture reporter"I'm the first person to be like, 'It's from M&S, you need to get on to it,'" Farron Clark, a 26-year-old brand strategist tells me. She says it's officially cool to buy your clothes from the high street retailer now.According to Clark and others on social media, Marks and Spencer is becoming the hot place to shop for women under 35, while also keeping its core older audience happy too. "For a long time M&S had this fusty reputation - it was less valued by younger people," says Chioma Nnadi, head of editorial content at British Vogue, who tells the BBC there is now a "fresh energy around the brand".And accompanying that fresh energy is a new marketing strategy, which includes hosting its first-ever London Fashion Week show on Friday, featuring a collection of outfits inspired by the brand's archive.So how is M&S attracting and retaining a younger generation of shoppers in a highly competitive market? The BBC went to the catwalk show and spoke to experts to find out.Image source, Reuters/Getty ImagesSpeaking ahead of the event at the Design Museum, the company's head of womenswear design, Lisa Illis, says they wanted to do this because of the "immediacy of seeing something and being able to own it and wear it, rather than waiting six months".For many, M&S is more synonymous with pig-shaped sweets than cutting-edge fashion, but its runway of 43 womenswear and 10 menswear looks did a lot to persuade people that the latter is where its true talent lie.Normally Fashion Week is about seeing what you'll be wearing six months from now, but this runway was full of colder weather fits, from opulent faux fur jackets and wrist cuffs, to satin jumpsuits and dresses in rich tones of navy, burgundy and brown.The catwalk featured a diverse range of models in age, size and gender, demonstrating the brand's desire to cater to a wide market. But there was certainly a concerted effort to attract the eye of younger shoppers with a fashion-forward approach to Christmas party staples like sequinned dresses, tasselled skirts and see-through lace tops.'They have created a modern version of everything we know and love'Image source, M&SImage caption, Womenswear and menswear collections at London Fashion Week are inspired by the M&S archiveThe retailer has been focusing on "newer styles and relevant trends" to attract younger customers, says Illis.But she says that this has been achieved without compromising on quality which is what keeps M&S's core audience on board."They have created a modern version of everything we know and love - cashmere staples, knitwear and the lingerie department," says Nnadi. Clark agrees that M&S has been nailing "funnel neck [styles] and barrel jeans, which are filtering down from high fashion".M&S has perhaps been fortunate to rebrand at a time when consumer habits are changing, as young shoppers consider buying capsule wardrobes - a smaller number of staple pieces that can be styled in a variety of ways. Clark notes that the idea of wear-it-once fast fashion has declined as people  "are looking for [foundational pieces] to rotate".This is something Perrie Sian, one of Britain's biggest fashion influencers, has also noticed. The 34-year-old tells the BBC: "The real height of fast fashion is behind us"."As a group we've changed our shopping habits and M&S slots into that," she says. "In my content and with lots of other creators we're showing people how to wear things in multiple ways, how to look after them."She added that she is noticing "people are willing to spend a little bit more" on wardrobe staples and items that "wash well and are made of cotton, not acrylic or polyester".Image source, Getty Images'Having a walk around M&S with my friends is the perfect Saturday'During the Covid pandemic M&S struggled, but returned to growth in 2022-2023, with its fashion, home and beauty market share reaching 9.6%.This again increased in 2023-2024 to 10%, and 10.5% in 2024-2025.But the business took a big hit in 2025 due to a cyber attack, which left shoppers unable to use its website and app and affected stock in stores too.It means M&S's market share on fashion, home and beauty now sits at 10.2%, external for 2025-26.Nnadi says M&S has been investing heavily in its retail spaces in recent years, focusing on "accessible luxury" with stores that feel "welcoming, new and fresh".And that's something Clark has noticed too."Getting an iced coffee and having a walk around M&S with my friends is the perfect Saturday," she says. "My generation do so much sitting on our phones, so an in-person experience becomes a bit of an activity." 'I'm getting straight to M&S'Image source, ReutersAccording to Sian, M&S has also taken "more risks" recently, which has helped it "create viral moments", including hosting a pit-lane fashion show at this year's F1 British Grand Prix and collaborating with British designers and creators."I'm seeing on Instagram or TikTok somebody say, 'Oh my goodness, this faux leather jacket is from M&S and it looks like it's £500 from the runway.' "And what am I doing? I'm hop, skip, jumping into my car and getting straight to my local M&S to hunt it down," Sian jokes. "They have embraced young designers like Marco Capaldo, the founder and creative director of 16Arlington," adds Nnadi. "And the Aries collab was genius and unexpected - it's a brand that has a lot of fashion kudos and is very British in its aesthetic but represents a younger vision of what British cool looks like," she says.Clark agrees the brand has "homed in on experts in their craft, rather than partnering with a million different people" like other fashion brands have made the mistake of doing.She notes their recent partnership with Stormzy's stylist Melissa Holbrook-Akposoe, who goes by Melissa's Wardrobe on social media, as "adding credibility" for younger shoppers.
